newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Stasi colonel's arms trade conviction upheld.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Stasi colonel's arms trade conviction upheld.

text.p: Germany's Federal Court of Justice on Wednesday upheld a 1996 conviction of former East Berlin secret police colonel Alexander Schalck-Golodkowski, found guilty of smuggling arms into communist East Germany.

Schalck, whose shadowy hard currency deals kept the former country afloat, had appealed against his conviction for illegally importing firearms and night-vision devices worth 8.5 million marks ($5.5 million) during the Cold War.
A former officer in the notorious Stasi secret police, Schalck still faces charges on other arms offences, fraud and misusing state funds to procure luxury Western goods for East German leaders.

Schalck was found guilty of procuring machines and components for producing microchips whose sale to the former East Bloc was outlawed by Western countries intent on keeping sensitive military technology out of their communist enemies' hands. He received an 18-month suspended jail sentence.

His lawyers however challenged the conviction, arguing that as a former East German citizen he could not be found guilty of breaking a Cold War law promulgated by Western victor powers which lapsed with unification in 1990.

They asked if East Germany could be expected to respect an arms embargo against itself. But Germany's highest criminal court ruled that his conviction for violating federal Geramn embargo law was not in conflict with the constitution.

Schalck inhabited a twilight world between the capitalist and communist spheres, heading a virtually impenetrable web of Western firms and contacts as head of East Berlin's shadowy Commercial Coordination (KoKo) department.

KoKo's main task was to rake in the billions of marks of hard currency which for years kept the ailing regime afloat. But it also existed to procure all the things East Germany most wanted, ranging from hi-tech goods to Western entertainment videos and luxury items for East Berlin's ageing rulers.
